lesson.title: The Parietal Lobe: Building a Map of Space and Body
lesson.summary: Sitting at the top and back of the brain, the parietal lobe processes touch and body sensation while constructing the brain's sense of where objects and body parts are in space.
lesson.body:
The parietal lobe occupies the upper back portion of the cerebral cortex, positioned behind the frontal lobe, above the temporal lobe, and in front of the occipital lobe. Like all four lobes of the cerebral cortex, it is duplicated on both the left and right sides of the brain, and each side contributes somewhat different specialties to the overall picture the brain builds of the body and the surrounding world. If the frontal lobe is largely about planning and acting, the parietal lobe is largely about knowing where things are, both in the world outside the body and within the body itself.

A strip of tissue at the very front edge of the parietal lobe, called the postcentral gyrus, contains the primary somatosensory cortex. This region receives incoming information about touch, pressure, temperature, and pain from receptors all over the skin, and it is organized in an orderly, almost map-like fashion, with different regions of cortex devoted to different body parts. Body parts with especially high sensitivity and fine motor control, such as the lips, tongue, and fingertips, take up disproportionately large amounts of cortical space compared to areas like the back or thigh, which is why a small paper cut on a fingertip can feel far more noticeable than a similarly sized scrape on a shoulder.

Beyond processing raw touch sensation, the parietal lobe integrates information from multiple senses to build a coherent, three-dimensional understanding of space, a function sometimes called spatial processing. This is what allows a person to reach accurately for a coffee cup without looking directly at their hand, to judge how far away a curb is before stepping off it, or to mentally rotate an object to figure out whether it will fit through a doorway. This spatial integration work relies on the parietal lobe combining visual input arriving from the occipital lobe with touch and body-position information arriving from its own somatosensory cortex.

The right parietal lobe in particular plays an outsized role in directing spatial attention across the entire visual field. Damage to this region, often from a stroke, can produce a striking and well-documented condition called hemispatial neglect, in which a person behaves as though the left side of space, and sometimes the left side of their own body, simply does not exist. A person with this condition might eat food from only the right half of a plate, groom only the right side of their face, or fail to notice objects placed on their left, even though their eyes and basic visual pathways are functioning normally. The disorder shows just how much ordinary spatial awareness depends on active processing by the parietal lobe rather than being an automatic byproduct of vision alone.

Because the parietal lobe sits at a crossroads between sensation, spatial cognition, and movement planning, it works in constant partnership with its neighboring lobes. It receives raw visual data forwarded from the occipital lobe and refines it into usable spatial information, then passes that spatial understanding forward to the frontal lobe so that intentions to reach, grasp, or navigate can be carried out accurately.
